source.title: The Forgotten Economists
source.summary: Did you know that a 14th-century Muslim scholar described supply and demand, the division of labor, and the labor theory of value, four hundred years before Adam Smith?
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Did you know that a 14th-century Muslim scholar described supply and demand, the division of labor, and the labor theory of value, four hundred years before Adam Smith? In this pilot episode, we trace the entire arc of Islamic economic thought: from the bustling markets of pre-Islamic Mecca and the Prophet Muhammad's career as a merchant, through the golden age of scholars like Abu Yusuf, Al-Ghazali, and Ibn Khaldun, to the colonial disruption and the remarkable modern revival of Islamic finance. Topics: Pre-Islamic Trade, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), Riba & Zakat, Golden Age Scholars, Ibn Khaldun, Trade Networks, Modern Revival Series: Historical Islamic Economics (Part I) • Episode 1 of 6

thread: Most people think economics began with Adam Smith. It actually began with Ibn Khaldun describing supply and demand in 14th-century Tunis.
The Prophet Muhammad was a merchant before he was a prophet. Abu Yusuf wrote about market regulation. Al-Ghazali explained the division of labor.
Islamic scholars were mapping trade networks from Mecca to China while Europe was still in the Dark Ages. They understood money, markets, and human behavior.
We call it the birth of economics. They were just solving the problems of their time. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-1

linkedin.post: Most people think economics began with Adam Smith in 1776. It actually began with Ibn Khaldun describing supply and demand in 14th-century Tunis—four hundred years earlier. The Prophet Muhammad was a merchant before he was a prophet. Abu Yusuf wrote about market regulation. Al-Ghazali explained the division of labor. These weren't abstract theories developed in isolation. They were practical solutions for managing vast trade networks that connected Mecca to China. Islamic scholars were mapping economic principles while Europe was still emerging from the Dark Ages. They understood money, markets, and human behavior because they lived it daily in the bustling souks of Baghdad, Cairo, and Cordoba. We've forgotten an entire tradition of economic thought that preceded and influenced what we now call classical economics. Listen to the full story: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-1
